content.intro: Learn ranking window functions through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Ranking Window Functions matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of ranking window functions is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

items.title: RANK
items.text: RANK is easier to reason about when the input row grain, partition keys, ordering, and tie-breaking rule are explicit. A window expression can add a calculation while keeping the individual input rows visible.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT department_id, full_name, salary,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS salary_rank
FROM employees
ORDER BY department_id, salary_rank, employee_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: Employees remain individual rows and receive a salary rank within each department; equal salary values share a DENSE_RANK.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
